1                             LEGAL STANDARD                              
2   I.   Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 12(b)(6)                         
3        Under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 12(b)(6), a district court must dismiss a complaint if 
4   it fails to state a claim upon which relief can be granted.  To survive a Rule 12(b)(6) motion to 
5   dismiss, the plaintiff must allege “enough facts to state a claim to relief that is plausible on its face.”  
6   Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544, 570 (2007).  This “facial plausibility” standard requires 
7   the plaintiff to allege facts that add up to “more than a sheer possibility that a defendant has acted 
8   unlawfully.”  Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662, 678 (2009).  While courts do not require “heightened 
9   fact pleading of specifics,” a plaintiff must allege facts sufficient to “raise a right to relief above the 
10   speculative level.”  Twombly, 550 U.S. at 555, 570.                   
11        In deciding whether the plaintiff has stated a claim upon which relief can be granted, the 
12   court must assume that the plaintiff’s allegations are true and must draw all reasonable inferences 
13   in the plaintiff’s favor.  Usher v. City of Los Angeles, 828 F.2d 556, 561 (9th Cir. 1987).  However, 
14   the court is not required to accept as true “allegations that are merely conclusory, unwarranted 
15   deductions of fact, or unreasonable inferences.”  In re Gilead Scis. Sec. Litig., 536 F.3d 1049, 1055 
16   (9th Cir. 2008).  A pleading must contain allegations that have “factual content that allows the court 
17   to draw the reasonable inference that the defendant is liable for the misconduct alleged.” Iqbal, 556 
18   U.S. at 678.  Dismissal under Rule 12(b)(6) is proper when the complaint “lacks a cognizable legal 
19   theory” or “fails to allege sufficient facts to support a cognizable legal theory.” Somers v. Apple, 
20   Inc., 729 F.3d 953, 959 (9th Cir. 2013).                              
21        If the Court dismisses the complaint, it must then decide whether to grant leave to amend. 
22   The Ninth Circuit has “repeatedly held that a district court should grant leave to amend even if no 
23   request to amend the pleading was made, unless it determines that the pleading could not possibly 
24   be cured by the allegation of other facts.”  Lopez v. Smith, 203 F.3d 1122, 1130 (9th Cir. 2000) 
25   (citations and internal quotation marks omitted).                     
26                                                                         
27   II.  Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 12(f)                            
1   “strike from a pleading an insufficient defense or any redundant, immaterial, impertinent, or 
2   scandalous matter.”   Fed. R. Civ. P. 12(f).  “[T]he function of a Rule 12(f) motion to strike is to 
3   avoid the expenditure of time and money that arises from litigating spurious issues by dispensing of 
4   those issues prior to trial.”  Sidney-Vinstein v. A.H. Robins Co., 697 F.2d 880, 885 (9th Cir. 1983).  
5   However, motions to strike are generally disfavored.  Rosales v. Citibank, Fed. Sav. Bank, 133 F. 
6   Supp. 2d 1177, 1180 (N.D. Cal. 2001).  Generally, a motion to strike “should not be granted unless 
7   the matter to be stricken clearly could have no possible bearing on the subject of the litigation.”  
8   Platte Anchor Bolt, Inc. v. IHI, Inc., 352 F. Supp. 2d 1048, 1057 (N.D. Cal. 2004).  “With a motion 
9   to strike, just as with a motion to dismiss, the court should view the pleading in the light most 
10   favorable to the nonmoving party.”  Id.

12                               DISCUSSION                                
13        Defendant brings the instant motion to dismiss plaintiff’s claim for declaratory relief and to 
14   strike the complaint’s request for relief relating to attorneys’ fees incurred prior to suit and pre- and-
15   post interest on any judgment.  Dkt. No. 27 at 1.  As plaintiff points out, at another point in its 
16   motion, defendant appears to also move to dismiss the request for attorneys’ fees.  See id. at 6.  The 
17   court thus evaluates whether plaintiff’s request for attorneys’ fees should be stricken under Rule 
18   12(f) or dismissed under Rule 12(b)(6).                               
19                                                                         
20   I.   Whether Plaintiff’s Claim for Declaratory Relief Should Be Dismissed 
21        Defendant contends that the complaint is “void of any allegations whatsoever suggesting 
22   that SVB was indeed in a contractual relationship with [p]laintiff and that SVB failed to perform 
23   prior to the bank failing and FDIC taking over as receiver.”  Dkt. No. 27 at 8.  Plaintiff responds 
24   that  this  argument  misses  the  point  because  its  “request  for  declaratory  relief  is  based  on 
25   [d]efendant’s partial disallowance of the claim, not the contract between plaintiff and SVB,” and 
26   defendant cites no legal authority that suggests that a plaintiff must plead privity of contract with 
27   the failed financial institution to file a declaratory relief claim against the FDIC as receiver.  Dkt. 
1   “Pursuant to 12 U.S.C. Section 1821(d)(6), if you do not agree with this disallowance, you have the 
2   right to file a lawsuit on your claim[.]”  Dkt. No. 4, Ex. D.         
3        The Court first addresses whether plaintiff must allege the existence of a written contract 
4   between it and SVB.  12 U.S.C. § 1821(d)(9)(A) states: “Except as provided in subparagraph (B) 
5   [which is not applicable here], any agreement which does not meet the requirements set forth in 
6   section 1823(e) of this title shall not form the basis of, or substantially comprise, a claim against the 
7   receiver or the Corporation.”  Section 1823(e) provides in general: “No agreement which tends to 
8   diminish or defeat the interest of the Corporation in any asset acquired by it under this section or 
9   section 1821 of this title . . . as receiver of any insured depository institution, shall be valid against 
10   the Corporation unless such agreement” meets a list of requirements, including being in writing.  12 
11   U.S.C. § 1821(e)(1).  The Ninth Circuit has explained that § 1823(e) “codified the policy embodied 
12   in the D’Oench, Duhme [doctrine],” which “is a principle of equitable estoppel that permits bank 
13   examiners to rely on the records of a bank in evaluating the bank’s financial condition, by protecting 
14   the  bank  authorities  from  suits  founded  on  undisclosed  conditions  or  deceptive  documents.”  
15   Brookside Associates v. Rifkin, 49 F.3d 490, 493 (9th Cir. 1995). The Ninth Circuit has further 
16   explained that:                                                       
          D’Oench, Duhme expresses a federal policy to protect the [FDIC] from misrepresentations 
17                                                                         
          concerning the assets of insured banks.  When a debtor asserts a “secret agreement” not in 
18         the records of the bank, whether to avoid enforcement of a note or in a suit such as this one 
          based on fraud in the inducement of an obligation, the D'Oench, Duhme policy favors the 
19         interests of bank examiners, as well as the agency that insures the bank, over debtors, who 
          can protect themselves against harm by making sure all of the terms of their agreements 
20         are in writing.                                                 
    Id. at 495.                                                           
21                                                                         
         The FDIC contends that a claim based on an oral agreement would not survive the FDIC’s 
22                                                                         
    claims process, only a written contract executed by the failed bank.  Dkt. No. 30 at 4.  The FDIC 
23                                                                         
    refers the Court to two cases in support of its position.             
24                                                                         
         In Langley v. Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation, the Supreme Court granted the 
25                                                                         
    defendants’ petition for certiorari “on the issue whether, in an action brought by the FDIC in its 
26                                                                         
    corporate capacity for payment of a note, § 1823(e) bars the defense that the note was procured by 
27                                                                         
1   86, 90 (1987).  The Court first determined the meaning of the word “agreement” in section 1821(e), 
2   finding that the common meaning of the word must be assigned to its usage if section 1823(e) “is to 
3   fulfill its intended purposes,” which the Court then reviewed.  See id. at 91-93.  The Court next 
4   concluded that “neither fraud in the inducement nor knowledge by the FDIC is relevant to the 
5   section’s application.”  Id. at 93.  The Court ultimately concluded:  “A condition to payment of a 
6   note, including the truth of an express warranty, is part of the ‘agreement’ to which the writing, 
7   approval, and filing requirements of 12 U.S.C. § 1823(e) attach.  Because the representations alleged 
8   by [the defendants] constitute such a condition and did not meet the requirements of the statute, they 
9   cannot be asserted as defenses here.”  Id. at 96.  The facts of Langley are not analogous to the present 
10   case, and the Court does not find that Langley provides a clear answer to whether plaintiff here must 
11   allege an “agreement” that meets the statutory requirements of § 1823(e).  
12        In MBIA Insurance Corporation v. F.D.I.C., the issue on an appeal of a motion to dismiss 
13   was “whether payments made by the [plaintiff] to investors in mortgage securitizations of a failed 
14   bank . . . constitute ‘administrative expenses’ entitled to priority” under the Financial Institutions 
15   Reform, Recovery, and Enforcement Act of 1989 (“FIRREA”).  708 F.3d 234, 235 (D.C. Cir. 2013).  
16   The plaintiff had sued a third-party beneficiary of Pooling and Servicing Agreements (“PSAs”) of 
17   a failed bank, alleging that the FDIC as conservator of the successor bank had “approved” the PSAs 
18   and then breached its obligations under those agreements, resulting in investor claims on plaintiff-
19   issued insurance policies.  Id. at 235.  The court assessed the plaintiff’s contention that its damages 
20   constitute “administrative expenses” entitled to priority under the statute because the FDIC had 
21   “approved” the PSAs within the meaning of the statute.  Id. at 236.  After an extensive statutory 
22   interpretation analysis, the court concluded that “contract approval demands a formal determination 
23   of necessity by the FDIC as Conservator or Receiver . . . and that a writing protects all interested 
24   parties,  distinguishing  ‘approved’  contracts  from  on-going  agreements  assumed  and  non-
25   repudiated.”  Id. at 245.  It further held that the plaintiff was not entitled to an “administrative 
26   expenses” distribution priority.  Id. at 247.  This case also does not provide guidance to the Court 
27   on whether plaintiff here must allege the existence of a written contract.          
1   asserted against FDIC in its capacity as receiver, regardless of whether the agreement is in writing 
2   or not.”  Dkt. No. 30 at 5.  In support, defendants point to Sharpe v. F.D.I.C., 126 F.3d 1147 (9th 
3   Cir. 1997).                                                           
4        In Sharpe, the Ninth Circuit held that the plaintiff’s damages claim was not affected by the 
5   12 U.S.C. §1821(j) jurisdictional bar, “but the claims for recission and declaratory relief must fall 
6   under an exception to § 1821(j) to survive.”  Id. at 1154-55.  Section 1821(j), “an anti-injunction 
7   section,” provides that:                                              
         Except as otherwise provided in this section, no court may take any action, except at 
8                                                                         
         the request of the Board of Directors by regulation or order, to restrain or affect the 
9        exercise of powers or functions of the Corporation as a conservator or a receiver. 
    12 U.S.C. § 1821(j).  The court found that the “FDIC failed to perform its obligations under the 
10                                                                         
    contract” at issue (a settlement agreement) and went on to address whether the FIRREA “imposes 
11                                                                         
    any limitation on [the plaintiffs’] state law right to pursue the action.”  Id. at 1152-54.  The court 
12                                                                         
    explained that section 1821(j) “bars restraint by the courts on the statutory powers of the FDIC when 
13                                                                         
    it acts as receiver” and “prevents courts from granting any equitable relief against the FDIC.”  Id. 
14                                                                         
    (citation omitted).  There are “few exceptions to this jurisdictional bar,” one of which is that the bar 
15                                                                         
    “does not extend to situations in which the FDIC as receiver asserts authority beyond that granted 
16                                                                         
    to it as receiver.”  Id. at 1154-55.  Specifically, “FIRREA does not authorize the breach of contracts” 
17                                                                         
    and “does not preempt state law so as to abrogate state law contract rights.”  Id. at 1155.  The FDIC 
18                                                                         
    “can escape the obligations of contracts, [but] it may do so only through the prescribed mechanism” 
19                                                                         
    of section 1821(e), which “allows the FDIC to disaffirm or repudiate any contract it deems 
20                                                                         
    burdensome and pay only compensatory damages.”  Id.  Because “the FDIC did not act within its 
21                                                                         
    statutorily granted powers in breaching the [plaintiffs’] settlement agreement,” the Court concluded 
22                                                                         
    that the plaintiff’s claims for declaratory relief and recission were not barred by section 1821(j).  Id.  
23                                                                         
    The Court does not find Sharpe dispositive on whether section 1821(j) bars plaintiff’s claim for 
24                                                                         
    declaratory relief here.                                              
25                                                                         
         MBIA Insurance Corporation held that the plaintiff’s request for declaratory and injunctive 
26                                                                         
    relief based on untimely repudiation was barred by section 1821(j).  708 F.3d at 247.  The plaintiff 
27                                                                         
1   FDIC Receivers” and a declaratory judgment that the FDIC failed to repudiate a Pooling and 
2   Servicing Agreement within a “reasonable period” as required by 12 U.S.C. § 1821(e)(2).  Id. at 
3   246-47.  The court explained that the FDIC as receiver or conservator is authorized to “disaffirm or 
4   repudiate any contract or lease . . . and therefore repudiation is properly viewed as a power of the 
5   Corporation acting in such capacities.”  Id. at 247 (citations and internal quotation marks omitted).  
6   “A court declaring a repudiation invalid would necessarily ‘restrain or affect the exercise’ of this 
7   power by the FDIC and thereby contravene § 1821(j).”  Id.  Here, plaintiff is not asking the court to 
8   declare a repudiation of a contract invalid but rather to review the FDIC’s partial disallowance of 
9   its claims.                                                           
10        Plaintiff contends that 12 U.S.C. § 1821(d)(6) is an exception to section 1821(j) that is 
11   appliable here.  The FDIC disagrees.  Case law from around the country supports plaintiff’s position.  
12   The Eleventh Circuit has explained that “Congress contemplated the reality that the FDIC may err 
13   in its determination of receivership claims and provided all claimants with the remedy of de novo 
14   review in federal court of the FDIC’s claims determination.”  Bank of America Nat. Ass’n v. Colonial 
15   Bank, 604 F.3d 1239, 1244 (11th Cir. 2010) (citing 12 U.S.C. § 1821(d)(6) and (d)(7)(A)).  Although 
16   it held under the facts of that case that the plaintiff’s claim was precluded by section 1821(j), it went 
17   on to explain that the operation of section 1821(j) does not leave the plaintiff without a remedy, 
18   because the claim could be pursued through the administrative claims process, and if not honored 
19   there, the plaintiff “has a statutory right to de novo review in federal district court.”  Id. at 1246-47.  
20   The Seventh Circuit has similarly held that “where the FDIC as receiver has disallowed a claim 
21   pursuant to the administrative process outlined in Section 1821(d) . . . the judicial resolution of that 
22   claim expressly permitted by that subsection should not typically run afoul of Section 1821(j).”  
23   Veluchamy v. F.D.I.C., 706 F.3d 810, 818 (7th Cir. 2013).  And the D.C. Circuit has explained that 
24   although section 1821(j) “does indeed effect a sweeping ouster of courts’ power to grant equitable 
25   remedies . . . serious due process concerns would be implicated if parties aggrieved by the FDIC’s 
26   actions as receiver were left entirely without remedies” and in many cases, “aggrieved parties will 
27   have opportunities to seek money damages or other relief through the administrative claims process 
1   Freeman v. F.D.I.C., 56 F.3d 1394, 1399 (D.C. Cir. 1995).             
2        Jafari v. F.D.I.C., No. 12cv2982-LAB (RBB), 2014 WL 1600441 (S.D. Cal. Apr. 18, 2014) 
3   is also instructive.  There, a California district court on a motion to dismiss distinguished cases 
4   finding that section 1821(j) prevents courts from granting equitable remedies against the FDIC on 
5   the grounds that those cases did not include a demand for monetary damages.  Id. at *3.  The plaintiff 
6   wanted to hold the FDIC to its offer to reconvey a deed of trust for $135,000, which implied the 
7   return of $3,649,067.10 paid to the FDIC by a third party.  Id.  The court reasoned that the plaintiff’s 
8   claims arguably sounded more in law than in equity, and that whether section 1821(j) barred the 
9   plaintiff’s claims “isn’t a matter of the labels affixed to them, but rather the actual relief those claims 
10   seek and an analysis of whether that relief would affect the FDIC’s exercise of its powers.”  Id. at 
11   *4.  Although the plaintiff’s equitable subrogation claim did “sound in equity and seek certain 
12   declaratory relief,” the court determined that it was “ultimately a claim for money damages that 
13   follows on the heels of the FDIC’s denial of [the plaintiff’s] administrative claim.”  Id.  The same 
14   can be said here: although plaintiff seeks declaratory relief, it is ultimately seeking to recover the 
15   money that was disallowed in the FDIC’s notices of partial disallowance.   
16        Given this authority, the Court cannot conclude at this pleadings stage that it does not have 
17   jurisdiction to review the partial disallowance of plaintiff’s claims.  Defendant’s motion to dismiss 
18   plaintiff’s claim for declaratory relief is therefore DENIED.         
19                                                                         
20   II.  Plaintiff’s Request for Pre- and Post-Judgment Interest          
21        Defendant argues that sovereign immunity bars an award of interest against the FDIC.  Dkt. 
22   No. 27 at 7.   Plaintiff does not address this argument in its opposition, instead arguing that a motion 
23   to strike under Rule 12(f) is not the appropriate place to raise this argument.  Sovereign immunity 
24   “generally bars an award of interest  against a federal  agency ‘unless  Congress  affirmatively 
25   mandates that result[.]’”  Far West Fed. Bank, S.B. v. Office of Thrift Supervision-Dir., 119 F.3d 
26   1358, 1366 (9th Cir. 1997) (quoting Library of Congress v. Shaw, 478 U.S. 310, 316 (1986)); see 
27   also Battista v. F.D.I.C., 195 F.3d 1113, 1120 (9th Cir. 1999) (confirming that Far West held “that 
1   waived  FDIC’s  immunity  against  prejudgment  interest”  but  there  is  an  exception  when  the 
2   government agency has “assumed the status of a commercial enterprise.”  Far West, 119 F.3d at 
3   1366.  Unlike some other agencies such as the Postal Service, “the FDIC operates as a governmental, 
4   regulatory entity, not as a private commercial enterprise.”  Id.  “[B]ecause FDIC is not a commercial 
5   entity and because Congress has not explicitly waived its immunity against interest, FDIC is not 
6   subject to a prejudgment interest award.”  Id. at 1367.               
7        Although it may not be the perfect place procedurally to raise the sovereign immunity 
8   argument, it is clear under the above-mentioned authority that sovereign immunity bars an award of 
9   interest against the FDIC.  The function of a 12(f) motion to strike is served by addressing this issue 
10   at this time.  The Court therefore GRANTS FDIC’s motion to strike plaintiff’s request for pre- and 
11   post-judgment interest.  See Delino v. Platinum Cmty. Bank, No. 09-CV-00288-H (AJB), 2010 WL 
12   11508574, at *3 (S.D. Cal. June 9, 2010) (granting motion to strike the plaintiff’s request for pre- 
13   and post-judgment interest against the FDIC based on sovereign immunity).    
14                                                                         
15   III.  Plaintiff’s Request for Attorneys’ Fees                         
16        The FDIC contends that plaintiff’s “claim for attorneys’ fees is without merit” and that 
17   plaintiff points to no provision of federal law that entitles it to attorneys’ fees.  Dkt. No. 27 at 6.  
18   Plaintiff responds that “requests made in the prayer for relief are not considered part of the statement 
19   of the claim . . . when tested” under Rule 8.  Dkt. No. 19 at 6.      
20        A leading treatise explains that:                                
         The sufficiency of a pleading is tested by the Rule 8(a)(2) statement of the claim for 
21                                                                         
         relief and the demand for judgment is not considered part of the claim for that 
22        purpose.  Thus, the selection of an improper remedy in the Rule 8(a)(3) demand for 
         relief will not be fatal to a party’s pleading if the statement of the claim indicates the 
23        pleader may be entitled to relief of some other type.            
24   Wright & Miller, Federal Practice and Procedure § 1255 (3d ed. 2004).  The “test of a complaint 
25   pursuant to a motion to dismiss lies in the claim, not in the demand.”  Palantir Technologies, Inc. v. 
26   Palantir. net, Inc., No. C 10-04283 CRB, 2011 WL 3047327, at *3 (N.D. Cal. July 25, 2011) 
27   (citation omitted).  Here, the availability of an award of attorneys’ fees to plaintiff does not “control 
1   IEG BGS, 2013 WL 3149483, at *3 (S.D. Cal. June 17, 2013) (holding that requests for punitive 
2   damages provide no basis for dismissal under Rule 12(b)(6)).  The Court therefore DENIES 
3   defendant’s motion to dismiss plaintiff’s request for attorneys’ fees. 
4        Additionally, the Court has reviewed the cases defendant cites in its briefing and does not 
5   find that these cases support a position that attorneys’ fees against the FDIC are always precluded 
6   as a matter of law.  For example, in Federal Deposit Ins. Corp. v. Meo, the Ninth Circuit reversed a 
7   district court decision and remanded “for determination of reasonable attorneys’ fees to be awarded 
8   Meo against FDIC.”  505 F.2d 790, 793 (9th Cir. 1974).  Additionally, in Sharpe, the Ninth Circuit, 
9   while noting that the FDIC’s sovereign immunity barred an award of prejudgment interest, found 
10   that it was “unable to determine the attorney’s fees and costs due” to the plaintiff based on its 
11   consideration of the record.  126 F.3d at 1154.                       
12        The Court likewise DENIES defendant’s motion to strike the request for attorneys’ fees.  In 
13   Whittlestone, Inc. v. Handi-Craft Co., the Ninth Circuit held that “Rule 12(f) . . . does not authorize 
14   district courts to strike claims for damages on the ground that such claims are precluded as a matter 
15   of law.”  618 F.3d 970, 974-75 (9th Cir. 2010).  The defendant had argued that the plaintiff’s claim 
16   for lost profits and consequential damages in a breach of contract suit should be stricken from the 
17   complaint because such damages are precluded as a matter of law.  Id. at 972, 974.  The court held 
18   that this argument was better suited for a Rule 12(b)(6) or Rule 56 motion, reasoning that the 
19   defendant’s 12(f) motion “was really an attempt  to  have certain  portions of [the plaintiff’s] 
20   complaint dismissed or to obtain summary judgment against [the plaintiff] as to those portions of 
21   the suit.”  Id. at 974.  The court further reasoned that “[w]ere we to read Rule 12(f) in a manner that 
22   allowed litigants to use it as a means to dismiss some or all of the pleading . . . we would be creating 
23   redundancies within the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure . . .”  Especially given that defendant has 
24   not adequately supported it position that “the FDIC, when appointed as receiver over a failed bank, 
25   cannot be liable for attorneys’ fees as a penalty,” the Court agrees with plaintiff that it would be 
26   inappropriate to strike its request for attorneys’ fees at this pleadings stage.  See Dkt. No. 27 at 5.

1                             LEGAL STANDARD                              
2   I.   Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 12(b)(6)                         
3        Under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 12(b)(6), a district court must dismiss a complaint if 
4   it fails to state a claim upon which relief can be granted.  To survive a Rule 12(b)(6) motion to 
5   dismiss, the plaintiff must allege “enough facts to state a claim to relief that is plausible on its face.”  
6   Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly,
550 U.S. 544, 570
 (2007).  This “facial plausibility” standard requires 
7   the plaintiff to allege facts that add up to “more than a sheer possibility that a defendant has acted 
8   unlawfully.”  Ashcroft v. Iqbal,
556 U.S. 662, 678
 (2009).  While courts do not require “heightened 
9   fact pleading of specifics,” a plaintiff must allege facts sufficient to “raise a right to relief above the 
10   speculative level.”  Twombly,
550 U.S. at 555, 570
.                   
11        In deciding whether the plaintiff has stated a claim upon which relief can be granted, the 
12   court must assume that the plaintiff’s allegations are true and must draw all reasonable inferences 
13   in the plaintiff’s favor.  Usher v. City of Los Angeles,
828 F.2d 556, 561
 (9th Cir. 1987).  However, 
14   the court is not required to accept as true “allegations that are merely conclusory, unwarranted 
15   deductions of fact, or unreasonable inferences.”  In re Gilead Scis. Sec. Litig.,
536 F.3d 1049
, 1055 
16   (9th Cir. 2008).  A pleading must contain allegations that have “factual content that allows the court 
17   to draw the reasonable inference that the defendant is liable for the misconduct alleged.” Iqbal, 556 
18   U.S. at 678.  Dismissal under Rule 12(b)(6) is proper when the complaint “lacks a cognizable legal 
19   theory” or “fails to allege sufficient facts to support a cognizable legal theory.” Somers v. Apple, 
20   Inc.,
729 F.3d 953, 959
 (9th Cir. 2013).                              
21        If the Court dismisses the complaint, it must then decide whether to grant leave to amend. 
22   The Ninth Circuit has “repeatedly held that a district court should grant leave to amend even if no 
23   request to amend the pleading was made, unless it determines that the pleading could not possibly 
24   be cured by the allegation of other facts.”  Lopez v. Smith,
203 F.3d 1122, 1130
 (9th Cir. 2000) 
25   (citations and internal quotation marks omitted).                     
26                                                                         
27   II.  Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 12(f)                            
1   “strike from a pleading an insufficient defense or any redundant, immaterial, impertinent, or 
2   scandalous matter.”   Fed. R. Civ. P. 12(f).  “[T]he function of a Rule 12(f) motion to strike is to 
3   avoid the expenditure of time and money that arises from litigating spurious issues by dispensing of 
4   those issues prior to trial.”  Sidney-Vinstein v. A.H. Robins Co.,
697 F.2d 880, 885
 (9th Cir. 1983).  
5   However, motions to strike are generally disfavored.  Rosales v. Citibank, Fed. Sav. Bank,
133 F. 6
   Supp. 2d 1177, 1180 (N.D. Cal. 2001).  Generally, a motion to strike “should not be granted unless 
7   the matter to be stricken clearly could have no possible bearing on the subject of the litigation.”  
8   Platte Anchor Bolt, Inc. v. IHI, Inc.,
352 F. Supp. 2d 1048, 1057
 (N.D. Cal. 2004).  “With a motion 
9   to strike, just as with a motion to dismiss, the court should view the pleading in the light most 
10   favorable to the nonmoving party.”
Id.

24   not adequately supported it position that “the FDIC, when appointed as receiver over a failed bank, 
25   cannot be liable for attorneys’ fees as a penalty,” the Court agrees with plaintiff that it would be 
26   inappropriate to strike its request for attorneys’ fees at this pleadings stage.  See Dkt. No. 27 at 5.
